description: Genome sequencing reads an organism's entire genetic material. In 1995 a whole-genome shotgun method, which needed no prior physical map, gave the first complete genome of a free-living organism, the bacterium Haemophilus influenzae. The Human Genome Project declared completion in April 2003, though about 8 percent, mostly repetitive DNA, stayed unread until 2022. A finished rice genome followed in 2005.

claims: Finished rice genome published in 2005 by an international project

uncertainty: The 2001 draft was released alongside a competing private effort (Celera); the 2003 'complete' human sequence still had gaps, closed only in 2022. Plant genome completion dates differ by source (rice: completed 2004, published 2005).

description: Gene editing changes a chosen DNA sequence inside living cells. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier's teams showed that Cas9, an enzyme from a bacterial defence system against viruses, could be guided by designed RNA to cut DNA at a chosen site, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Rules for edited crops differ between countries.

claims: Genome editing modifies specific sites in DNA
Legal status of edited crops unclear in some jurisdictions
Regulation of CRISPR-edited crops differs between countries (US clearance 2016)

uncertainty: Priority is contested: Virginijus Siksnys's group reported similar Cas9 results in 2012, and patent disputes over use in human cells (Broad Institute, 2013 work) followed. CRISPR repeats were noticed in bacteria in 1987 and their immune role was established only in 2005-2007.

description: A catalytic converter passes engine exhaust over a platinum-bearing catalyst that speeds reactions cleaning it. Under the 1970 Clean Air Act, new United States cars carried converters from the 1975 model year; these early units oxidised carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons. Lead coats the catalyst, so unleaded petrol spread alongside. Three-way converters, which also reduce nitrogen oxides, followed from 1977.

claims: Lead coats catalyst; 1975 model year; Clean Air Act; platinum

uncertainty: Exhaust catalysts were patented earlier (Eugene Houdry, 1950s) but not adopted until emission law required them; adoption dates differ by country (Japan and Europe later than or alongside the US), so 1975 marks the US mass fitting.

description: Carbon capture separates carbon dioxide from gas streams for use or storage. In amine scrubbing, used since about 1930 to remove carbon dioxide from natural gas and hydrogen, an amine solution binds the gas chemically. At Norway's Sleipner field, amines strip carbon dioxide from produced gas for storage, a process its operator found costly to develop.
uncertainty: Whether capture can reach climate-relevant scale is unresolved (the node's 'scale speculative'); most captured CO2 historically went to enhanced oil recovery. The 1930 patent (R. R. Bottoms), early-1970s Texas projects and Sleipner's 1996 start are standard histories not confirmed by credible results in this pass.

description: DNA sequencing reads the order of the four bases along a DNA strand. Two methods were reported in 1977: Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert's chemical cleavage, and Frederick Sanger's chain termination, which used modified nucleotides that halt DNA copying. That year Sanger's group also published the first complete DNA genome, of the virus phiX174, over 5,000 bases long.

claims: Dideoxy chain-terminating inhibitors; applied to phiX174
Two methods in 1977; first complete genome phiX174

uncertainty: The node's range 1975-1977 covers Sanger's earlier 'plus and minus' method (1975), which was used for phiX174; the chain-termination method followed in 1977. RNA sequences had been read earlier (1960s), so 'first reading of genetic text' applies to DNA methods specifically.
